cards.title: Test process at a glance
cards.summary: A lookup sequence, not a waterfall: activities overlap, repeat, and feed each other.

rows.detail: Define objectives, approach, resources, schedule, risks, and completion criteria.
Compare actual progress/status with plan and adjust when needed.
Study the test basis and identify what needs to be tested: test conditions.
Turn conditions into test cases, coverage items, expected results, and data needs.
Prepare procedures/scripts, suites, data, environment, and execution order.
Run tests, compare actual vs expected, log evidence, analyze anomalies.

moreRows.detail: Consolidate results, unresolved risks, lessons, assets, and closure reporting.
If execution is failing repeatedly, check whether analysis/design/data/environment was weak upstream.

Required account, permissions, configuration, state, build, or dependencies.
Exact inputs or a clear generation rule; include boundary/invalid values when relevant.
Minimal reproducible steps or API operation.

cards.summary: Before designing cases, make the requirement observable enough to test. Ambiguity found here is cheaper than ambiguity found in execution.

Ranges, defaults, rounding, limits, ordering, duplicates, timeouts, retries.

moreRows.detail: Performance, accessibility, security, reliability, compatibility, privacy, safety where relevant.

cards.title: Test oracle: how do you know it is correct?
cards.summary: When expected results are unclear, identify the source of truth before adding more tests.

rows.detail: Explicit business rule or acceptance criterion.
Trusted existing implementation, simulator, or previous validated version.
Recompute using a separate formula/model rather than duplicating implementation logic.
Property that must always hold, e.g. totals balance or IDs stay unique.
Law, standard, protocol, accounting rule, medical/business domain constraint.

moreRows.detail: Useful for UX, visual quality, exploratory testing; define reviewer expectations where possible.

cards.title: Equivalence Partitioning
cards.summary: Split a domain into groups expected to behave alike, then test representative members.

rows.detail: Example: allowed age is 18–65.
Valid: 18–65. Invalid: <18. Invalid: >65.
Example: 30, 17, 66. One representative per partition is the minimum idea, not always enough.
exercised partitions ÷ identified partitions × 100%.

moreRows.detail: Partition each field, then use risk/combination techniques instead of testing every Cartesian product.
Values belong to one partition only if you have reason to expect equivalent behavior.

searchTerms: equivalence classes partitions valid invalid partition coverage

cards.title: Boundary Value Analysis
cards.summary: Focus on borders because implementation mistakes often occur at inclusive/exclusive limits.

rows.detail: For valid 18–65, boundaries are 18 and 65.
Exercise each boundary and the closest value across it: 17, 18, 65, 66.
Exercise below / on / above each boundary: 17, 18, 19 and 64, 65, 66.
For x < 10, explicitly distinguish 9 from 10; do not treat 10 as valid.

moreRows.detail: Dates, lengths, list sizes, file sizes, pagination limits, retries, and quotas also have boundaries.
EP tells you the classes; BVA intensifies testing around their edges.

searchTerms: boundary min max off by one 2 value 3 value BVA

cards.title: Decision Tables
cards.summary: Use when combinations of conditions determine different actions or outcomes.

rows.detail: List independent inputs/rules, e.g. authenticated? account active? limit exceeded?
List observable outcomes, e.g. allow, deny, require verification.
Each feasible column is one combination of condition values and expected actions.
Merge combinations only when a condition truly does not affect the outcome (don't-care).
executed feasible rules ÷ identified feasible rules × 100%.

moreRows.detail: Remove impossible combinations only with a justified domain rule.
If requirements contain many if/and/or/unless statements, a decision table is often clearer than prose.

cards.title: State Transition Testing

Current state + event → next state + observable action.
Exercise required transitions and meaningful multi-step sequences.
Try events that must be rejected or ignored from a given state.

cards.title: Statement vs branch coverage
cards.summary: Coverage tells you what structure was exercised, not whether assertions or requirements were adequate.

rows.detail: executed executable statements ÷ total executable statements × 100%.
executed branches ÷ total branches × 100%.
100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage for the measured code; the reverse is not guaranteed.
An if statement may execute its body and reach 100% statements while never testing the false branch.

moreRows.detail: Use uncovered branches as investigation prompts, not automatic proof that each deserves a test.
High coverage can coexist with weak assertions, missing requirements, and wrong test data.

cards.title: Confirmation vs regression
cards.summary: First prove the reported failure is fixed; then ask what else the change could have broken.

rows.detail: Re-run the failed scenario and relevant variants against the fixed build.

Changed code/config + dependencies + shared data + interfaces + adjacent business flows.
Prioritize high-impact and high-likelihood consequences, not the entire historical suite by default.

moreRows.detail: A defect can be correctly fixed while introducing a new failure elsewhere.
Stable repeated regression is a strong automation candidate; exploratory follow-up still adds value for risky changes.

Revenue, safety, security, data loss, legal exposure, user volume, blocked core task, recovery cost.
Test earlier, with stronger techniques, broader data, more independence, and more regression.

cards.title: Entry, exit & stop criteria
cards.summary: Criteria should trigger decisions; they are not ceremonial checklists.

rows.detail: Conditions to start useful testing: build deployable, environment/data ready, scope/basis available, blockers understood.
Evidence needed to consider the objective sufficiently met: planned risk coverage, defect state, key results, residual risk.
Conditions that make continued execution wasteful or unsafe: broken environment, invalid build, blocking dependency.
Specific condition proving the blocker is resolved and test evidence can be trusted again.

moreRows.detail: 100% tests passed as a universal exit rule; it ignores missing tests, wrong scope, waived defects, and product risk.
Use criteria tied to critical flows, risk items, defect thresholds, required environments, and stakeholder acceptance.

cards.title: Release readiness
cards.summary: A release decision is a risk decision supported by evidence, not a single pass percentage.

rows.detail: Required journeys pass in the relevant release candidate/environment.
Changed areas and dependencies received appropriate confirmation/regression.
Known defects are understood by severity, exposure, workaround, and release impact.
Known untested/partially tested areas and assumptions are visible to decision-makers.
Monitoring, alerts, rollback/feature flag, support/runbook, migration/recovery where relevant.

cards.title: Metrics that answer a decision

Open/closed trend, severity, age, reopen rate, escaped defects where meaningful.
Requirements/risks/techniques/code areas covered; state what coverage means.
Flaky tests, environment failures, automation reliability, build/deploy health.

moreRows.detail: Number of test cases, bugs found, or automation percentage alone does not equal quality.
